messages.subject: Re: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes
messages.body_plain:
For one-sided hypothesis (e.g. x > 0), we get Inf, if all posterior samples of x are above zero. In this case, we have infinitely more posterior mass (as measured by posterior samples) above zero than below.

The only way to get a non-inf value in this case would be to approximate the histogram of the posterior samples with a smooth density, but this is not really what I would recommend doing.
Or you could run many more samples in the hope that some of them eventually fall below zero.

In such a case one might simply want to say that x > 0 is over 1000 (or more) times more likely than x <= 0.

messages.subject_clean: interpretation of ordinal regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

thanks for this package, its a good opportunity to learn and actually do Bayesian data analysis.
I'm working with acceptability rating data (discrete from 1 - 9) and therefore need to use ordinal regression (as I understand it).
Doing so works fine but also results in some questions regarding the interpretation of the coefficients

My current brms model -- simplified for this thread -- looks like this:

brm(Rating ~ metricPredictor + (1 | subject),
    family = cumulative, data = ratings)

Running this model and printing the summary gives me 8 intercepts and 1 slope parameters.
As I understood ordinal regression (mainly based on John Kruschke's DBDA book), the 8 intercepts are the thresholds of the underlying cumulative function (all prob. density below Intercept[0] is summed up to get the prob. for rating 1, all prob. density between Intercept[0] and Intercept[1] is summed and mapped to rating 2, etc.)
Since I have ratings ranging from 1 to 9, I get 8 thresholds.

Now some questions:
- are the thresholds actual intercepts of linear functions or are they named to be compatible with other models but actually they are thresholds for the pdf? I'm not sure, if this is clearly formulated, so I put the question in a different way: If the intercepts are intercepts from a linear function, I colud draw this linear function (x-axis: predictor, y-axis: rating). but why do I have more intercepts than slopes?
- I'm getting negative intercepts (aka threshold) but my rating data only allows positive ratings -- how does this fit?
- can I interpret the coefficient for metricPredictor as a slope of linear function on the same scale as the rating data? So, for example, if I have a coefficient of 3.5, can I interpret this in terms of "increasing metricPredictor by 1 unit leads to a higher rating of 3.5 (compared to the baseline)"?
- does the choice of the link function (logit by default) changes the way I should think about the coefficients? Kruschke uses in his book as explanation an underlying metric variable (see Figure 23.6, page 647, available from https://sites.google.com/site/doingbayesiandataanalysis/figures), but he explains that this underlying variable is normally distributed (and then cumulated into the distinct categories using the threshold). If I got this correct, his explanation leads to a probit link-function? Can I still use the explanation given by Kruschke if I'm using a logit function (which actually is quicker and fits the data better in terms of a pp_check).

Thanks in advance for an answer,
Thomas

There are two reasons for this at first glance strange code.

(a) It is sometimes faster. I am not fully sure about the cause, but I assume that repeatedly indexing elements of matrices (n times) is slower than extracting a column once and indexing a vector afterwards. At least I found examples, where it leads to 10-20% speed increase and never had an example where it was slower.

(b) It is easier to write Stan code for distributional models with group-level effects correlated across formulae. For instance, if you look at

data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
make_stancode(bf(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | ID | Subject),
                 sigma ~ Days + (Days | ID | Subject)),
                 sleepstudy)

you see that we can define more consistent parameter names.

Hi Thomas,

They are both thresholds and intercepts in the way that the thresholds happen to be the model intercepts in this parameterization.

In all your questions, don't forget that you are using a link function (logit by default as you correctly point out).

When assuming a normal distribution, you have to use the probit link. Using logit implies a logistisc distribution.

Paul

I'm building a model and wish to apply a random effect to all of the independent variables (the "combo" variable is the random effect). I have specified two models through BRMS, and I'm not sure why they work different. They're listed below:

fit_zinb1 <- brm(camShot ~ (race + cam + race*cam | combo) + (log(racePop+1)),
                 data = countyPoisson, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())

                       data = countyPoisson, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())

When I run the first model and print a summary, the output only lists group-level effects (a bunch of standard deviations and correlations amongst the independent variables). When I run the second model, the output lists population-level AND group-level effects. Can anyone shed light on why I'm getting such different results between the two models?

Thanks in advance!
-Hope

Hi Hope,

both models are completely different. The first model fits, as you point out, only random effects. Since they are centerd around zero, they are more or less meaningless without a corresponding fixed effect. Accordingly, you almost certainly want

fit_zinb3 <- brm(camShot ~ race + cam + race*cam + (race + cam + race*cam | combo) + (log(racePop+1)),
                 data = countyPoisson, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())

The second model has the fixed effects, but only a random intercept: (1 | combo).

If you want race, combo and their interaction to vary across combo, fit_zinb3 ist the way to go.

Best,
Paul

P.S. You can simplify the model specification without altering the output by writing

fit_zinb3 <- brm(camShot ~ race*cam + (race*cam | combo) + (log(racePop+1)),
                 data = countyPoisson, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())

as race*cam is expanded to race + cam + race:cam anyway (default R formula parsing)

messages.subject: Horseshoe prior on single coefficients?
messages.subject_clean: Horseshoe prior on single coefficients?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have one technical one one conceptual question, and would be interested in your thoughts.

First, conceptual:

We have a model where we have a set of theoretically relevant variables ("Set 1"). We want to retain them in the model, regardless whether they contribute to the prediction or not.
Furthermore, we have an additional set of control variables ("Set 2"). This is a large set of potential covariates, and we would only like to keep those which make a contribution, but still keep the model as simple as possible. Hence, Set 1 refers to confirmatory hypotheses, and Set 2 is exploratory (however, both are in the same model).

Our idea is to put a weakly informative prior on Set 1 (say, "normal(0, 1)" on standardized variables), and a more aggressive regularization (LASSO or horseshoe) on Set 2.

Does this make sense to you? Any pitfalls we might have overseen?

Second, technical:

The manual says: " The horseshoe prior can be applied on all population-level effects at once (excluding the intercept) by using set_prior("horseshoe(1)")". Is it also possible to set horseshoe or lasso priors on single parameters?

If not: is this an inherent limitation, a limitation of brms, or a limitation of STAN? Ideas for workarounds?

Thanks,
Felix

Hi Felix,

with the latest dev version of brms from github, you may try the following:

priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1), nlpar = "eta1")
            prior(horseshoe(), nlpar = "eta2"))
bformula <- bf(y ~ eta1 + eta2,
               eta1 ~ <set1 variables>,
               eta2 ~ 0 + <set2 variables>,
               nl = TRUE)
fit <- brm(bformula, <your data>, prior = priors)

The intercept of eta2 has to be removed or otherwise we will end up with two intercepts.
Please make sure not to use factors in <set2 variables> in order to avoid accidental cell mean coding.

I am curious to hear if this solutions works out for your examples.

Best,
Paul

Technically, it works (but it generates more divergent transitions than the other models).

Here's my code:
priors <- c(prior("normal(0, 1)", nlpar = "eta1"),
            prior("horseshoe(1)", nlpar = "eta2"))

bformula <- bf(y ~ eta1 + eta2,
               eta1 ~ age + sex + bmi + map + ldl + tch,
               eta2 ~ 0 + hdl + ltg + glu + tc,
               nl = TRUE)

# adapt delta due to divergent transitions after warmup
l.brm.horseshoeSet2 <- brm(bformula, data=df, prior = priors, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 4, cores=4, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999))

I used a demo data set "diabetes" from the lars package, and put hdl + ltg + glu + tc into set 2 with a horseshoe prior.

Intuitively, I would have expected that the Set-2 coefficients from the l.brm.horseshoeSet2 model (purple) are close to the coefficients from the global horseshoe model (blue) - this is not really the case:

In fact, the coefficients from the new feature seem a bit off. But I have to play around more to get a better understanding.

Cheers,
Felix

Let's say you are interested in the posterior mode of the population-level intercept. Then you can do the follwing:

# extract posterior samples
ps <- as.matrix(fit, "^b_Intercept$")
# compute the mode
estimate_mode <- function(x) {
  # quick and dirty way to compute the mode
  d <- density(x)
  d$x[which.max(d$y)]
}
estimate_mode(ps)
